topic: The Bridge Between Change and Accumulation: The Relationship Between Integrals and Derivatives
target_audience: First-year university students or advanced high school students

outline.topic: The Bridge Between Change and Accumulation: The Relationship Between Integrals and Derivatives
outline.target_audience: First-year university students or advanced high school students

sections.title: The Hook: The Cheetah's Dash (0:00 - 0:45)
sections.content: Introduce the two main branches of calculus through a physical scenario. Differentiation measures 'instantaneous change' (speedometer), while Integration measures 'total accumulation' (odometer). This section sets the stage for why we need to connect them.
sections.example: An animated Cheetah accelerates across the screen. Above it, a graph shows its velocity. We pose the question: If we know the Cheetah's velocity at every second (Derivative), can we figure out the total distance it traveled (Integral) without adding up infinite tiny steps?

sections.title: Prerequisite Refresh: Slopes and Slices (0:45 - 1:30)
sections.content: Briefly visualize the two operations independently. Differentiation as finding the slope of a tangent line; Integration as calculating the area under a curve using Riemann sums (thin rectangles).
sections.example: A split-screen animation. On the left, a magnifying glass zooms into a curve to show a straight-line slope (dy/dx). On the right, a curve is filled with increasingly thin vertical bars to represent the area.

sections.title: The Accumulation Function (1:30 - 2:30)
sections.content: Introduce the 'Area Function' A(x), which represents the area under a curve f(t) from a fixed point 'a' to a moving point 'x'. This is the 'bridge' concept. Explain that as 'x' moves, the area grows.
sections.example: A 'Scanning Bar' moves from left to right across a graph of f(t). As it moves, the region behind it is shaded, and a new graph A(x) is plotted simultaneously above it, showing the total shaded area growing over time.

sections.title: FTC Part 1: The Rate of Growth (2:30 - 3:30)
sections.content: Demonstrate the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Part 1. Show that the rate at which the area A(x) increases is exactly equal to the height of the function f(x) at that point. This proves that the derivative of an integral is the original function.
sections.example: Zoom into the edge of the scanning bar. Show a tiny increase in width (dx). The tiny increase in area (dA) is a rectangle of height f(x) and width dx. Visually demonstrate dA/dx = f(x) using a 'puzzle piece' metaphor where the height of the curve determines the speed of area growth.

sections.title: FTC Part 2: The Shortcut (3:30 - 4:30)
sections.content: Explain the Evaluation Theorem. If Integration and Differentiation are inverses, we can calculate the area under f(x) simply by finding its antiderivative F(x) and calculating F(b) - F(a). No more infinite sums needed.
sections.example: A 'Climb the Ladder' metaphor. To find the area under a velocity curve (f), we simply look at the height difference on the position ladder (F). The animation shows the area under a curve being 'poured' into a vertical cylinder to measure its height difference.

sections.title: Summary: The Symmetry of Calculus (4:30 - 5:00)
sections.content: Conclude by emphasizing the perfect symmetry. Differentiation 'breaks down' a function into its rates; Integration 'builds up' those rates into a total value. They are two sides of the same coin.
sections.example: A circular infographic showing a function f(x). An arrow pointing clockwise (differentiation) leads to f'(x), and an arrow pointing counter-clockwise (integration) leads back to f(x), forming a continuous loop of mathematical logic.

storyboard.title: The Hook: The Cheetah's Dash (0:00 - 0:45)
lecture_lines: A cheetah sprints, its velocity changing every second.
Differentiation tells us its speed at any moment.
Integration calculates the total distance the cheetah traveled.
animations: Cheetah silhouette (yellow: #FFFF00) moves from left to right across the screen.
Velocity graph (green: #00FF00) appears above the Cheetah, tracing its speed over time.
A speedometer icon (white: #FFFFFF) flashes to emphasize 'Differentiation' as instantaneous change.
An odometer icon (blue: #0000FF) appears, representing 'Integration' as total distance accumulated.
A question mark (white: #FFFFFF) appears between the speedometer and odometer icons.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Refresh: Slopes and Slices (0:45 - 1:30)
lecture_lines: Derivatives find the slope of a tangent line.
Integrals calculate the area under a curve.
Are these two mathematical operations somehow connected?
animations: A curve y = f(x) (red: #FF0000) appears with a tangent line slope shown at a single point.
Screen splits: the right side displays the same curve filled with cyan (#00FFFF) Riemann rectangles.
The rectangles become infinitely thin, merging into a smooth solid area under the curve.

storyboard.title: The Accumulation Function (1:30 - 2:30)
lecture_lines: Define the accumulation function as the area so far.
As the boundary moves, the shaded area grows.
We denote this area function as A(x).
A(x) tracks the total integral from start to x.
Watch how A(x) changes as we scan the curve.
animations: Function f(t) (yellow: #FFFF00) is plotted on a 2D plane with 'a' and 'x' marked on the axis.
A vertical scanning bar (white: #FFFFFF) starts at t = a and begins moving right.
The bar moves toward t = x, shading the area behind it in semi-transparent yellow (#FFFF00).
A new curve A(x) (blue: #0000FF) is drawn above the graph to track the total shaded area.
Labels 'f(t)' (yellow: #FFFF00) and 'A(x)' (blue: #0000FF) appear next to their respective curves.

storyboard.title: FTC Part 1: The Rate of Growth (2:30 - 3:30)
lecture_lines: Consider a tiny increase in the area, dA.
This narrow strip has a width of dx.
Its height is simply the function's value, f(x).
Thus, the rate of area growth is f(x).
The derivative of the integral is the original function.
animations: Zoom into the right edge of the shaded area A(x) at the specific point x.
The boundary moves a tiny distance Δx (white: #FFFFFF), creating a thin vertical slice.
The slice is highlighted as a rectangle with height f(x) (green: #00FF00) and width dx.
The equation dA = f(x) * dx appears in white (#FFFFFF) next to the slice.
The derivative notation d/dx [A(x)] = f(x) appears and flashes in bright white (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: FTC Part 2: The Shortcut (3:30 - 4:30)
lecture_lines: We can now evaluate integrals using antiderivatives.
If F is an antiderivative, the area is simple.
Just calculate the difference between the endpoints.
F(b) minus F(a) gives the exact total area.
This shortcut bypasses the need for infinite sums.
animations: A curve f(x) (orange: #FFA500) is shown with the area between boundaries a and b shaded.
The antiderivative function F(x) (magenta: #FF00FF) is plotted on a separate scale above f(x).
Vertical markers at a and b show the height difference F(b) - F(a) on the F(x) curve.

storyboard.title: Summary: The Symmetry of Calculus (4:30 - 5:00)
lecture_lines: Calculus reveals a beautiful symmetry in change.
Differentiation and integration are perfect inverses.
Together, they bridge the gap between change and accumulation.
animations: The text 'f(x)' appears in the center of the screen in white (#FFFFFF).
A red (#FF0000) arrow circles 'f(x)' clockwise, labeled 'Differentiate' to show the forward path.
A blue (#0000FF) arrow circles 'f(x)' counter-clockwise, labeled 'Integrate' to show the reverse path.
